#305. The 6 Best Latte Machines for Automatic Espresso Drinks (2026)

A latte is rich and milky heaven. A cappuccino is the cloud that heaven rests on. The best latte machines and the best automatic espresso machines are the ones that can give you this richness consistently, easily, and deliciously. Home espresso machines, like the classic devices in our guide to the Best Espresso Machines, often have a reputation for being intimidating. But they don't have to be.

Some machines make it easy and keep you from having to drive to the coffee shop. The automatic espresso machines in this guide can make a perfect frothy cappuccino accessible with the press of a single button, or maybe a couple of buttons. Our top high-end superautomatic espresso machine, the De'Longhi Rivelia (7/10, WIRED Recommends), is a paragon of easy-peasy, frothy, pleasing cappuccinos and flat whites. The new Ninja Cafe Luxe Pro (see here on Amazon) seems determined to produce every kind of coffee in existence.

Most of the machines on this list also come with grinders, but our guide to The Best Coffee Grinders may also be helpful. For more WIRED coffee coverage, check out our guides to The Best Coffee Subscriptions, The Best Drip Coffee Machines, The Best Milk Frothers, and The Best Cold Brew Makers, or look for our recent coffee gear reviews.

Updated November 2026: We’ve added information on WIRED UK’s blind taste test of popular fully automatic bean-to-cup machines and ensured up-to-date links and prices.

A sophisticated bean-to-cup machine from Italian coffee titan De'Longhi, the Rivelia (7/10, WIRED Recommends) immediately ranks among the most modern, impressive, user-friendly, and capable superautomatic espresso machines I’ve encountered—the sort that has you dump a half-bag of beans into a hopper and will grind, brew, then froth up milk for a flat white, amid 18 options on espresso, latte, cappuccino, and iced-coffee drink options.

Pretty much everything operates via an easy touchscreen, including bean guidance that lets you optimize the machine for each bean. The milk frother works at the press of a button and makes actual microfoam—and the foam’s density can be adjusted to make a frothier cappuccino or dense flat white. It’s so easy I let my parents test-drive it, and they fell in love with it within a day. If you’ve got multiple people using the machine, you can save multiple profiles and your favorite custom drinks. So Dad can have his basic “coffee” that’s actually a European-style café crema, and Mom can have her ridiculously large 16-ounce travel-mug latte. (Yes, these are their drinks.)

What's better, the Rivelia has two swappable bean hoppers, so it’s easy to swap between caff and decaf, or between light and dark roasts. Honestly, this is the bean-to-cup espresso machine that fully sold me on the idea of automatic coffee machines like this one. Though note: Fully automatic espresso machines like the Rivelia grind a little coarser, in order to make espresso less finicky and less difficult. This leads to a smoother but less nuanced profile than espresso shots you’d find in a café. But if you're a milk lover, the absolute ease with which the Rivelia froths a cappuccino will likely balance this out. The cold espresso is also a pleasant option when mixed with milk or vodka.

A lot of machines can make you a cloudy, clumpy, big-bubble cappuccino without much hassle. But it's that well-integrated microfoam, the silkiness, that feels like an actual luxury—elevates a good foamed milk from the merely milky latte to silly morning ecstasy.

There's a lot to like about Ninja's flagship entry into the espresso market: in particular, dosing by weight and an easy bean guidance function that actually helps in dialing in a bean. Quite simply, this machine offers real-deal, unpressurized portafilter espresso without the fussiness. But what I especially like about this Ninja is the milk. Some superautomatic machines have tube-filled, plasticky milk systems that are annoying to clean. Some never get a fine froth. This Ninja Luxe Cafe Pro is the best of each world, a steam wand and stainless steel steamer cup with a spinning whisk at its bottom that simulates the whirlpool created by a skilled barista. Whether cold foam or hot foam, Ninja's Luxe Cafe series offers truly excellent foam for your morning cup.

Now, for this: It is not a superautomatic machine like the Rivelia, though it’s among the easiest portafilter machines I've ever used. The conical burr grinder is built in, it doses accurately, the tamper handle is easy, and bean guidance will tell you what to do without much fuss. Mostly, you just need to transfer the portafilter from one spot on the machine to another.

Note that for a lower price, the Ninja Luxe Cafe Premier (described below) offers the same great milk froth, but you lose the automatic tamper and a hot water spout. For me, the Pro is the pick for a more pleasant morning and greater versatility. Note that while the massive drip tray does hold a lot of water, it’s a bit of a production to empty and replace, and that while it also purports to be a drip coffee maker, it’s nothing to write your mother about.

This Mr. Coffee machine was once our top pick for lattes. Why? Because it sits so nicely at a comfortable intersection where ease of use meets automation and affordability. This is about the lowest-priced machine you can ever expect to find with automatic milk frothing at the press of a single button, with options for latte foam or cappuccino froth. Just load fine-ground coffee into the portafilter, tamp it down, and twist it on. The machine will mix up a cappuccino or a latte macchiato at the press of a button.

This machine has a forgiving (but not overly intense or nuanced) pressurized portafilter, which means it will work with almost any “espresso-grind” coffee from your local café or the grocery store. Just note you’ll still get a better shot of espresso if you buy a grinder and use fresh beans from a good specialty roaster. But all in all, this is about the easiest $200 latte machine we know. Like, the hardest thing about it is that the milk canister can be removed and stored in the fridge, and you have to clean it out once a week.

The Cafe Affetto is one of the few fully automatic machines that WIRED has enjoyed in this price range. The Affetto features a built-in steaming wand, produces 20 bars of pump pressure to ensure your espresso is fully extracted, and is a slick little machine. It’s very slim and fits comfortably on a small apartment countertop without having to rearrange everything. Because coffee production is automated, you just need to fill the water tank and put whole beans in the hopper, and you’re good to go. You can brew one or two shots with just the press of a button, and there’s a programmable button to create your favorite drinks (like an Americano with just the right amount of water).

The milk frother does a lot of the work on its own. Just pour some of your favorite milk into the frothing pitcher, submerge the wand, and hit the steam button. If you’re new to frothing milk, you don't even need to move the pitcher to produce a creamy and consistent microfoam. WIRED reviewer Jaina Grey tested the frother with dairy milk, oat milk, and soy milk, and found it produced soft and creamy café-grade froth each time. Just make sure it’s topped up with water and beans and that you clean out the spent grounds container regularly, and it works like a dream.

The Breville Oracle Jet (8/10, WIRED Recommends) is my favorite of the two dozen or so new espresso machines I’ve tried so far this year. It’s the one I recommend as my top pick in WIRED’s guide to the Best Espresso Machines, over other estimable contenders from Breville that include the Barista Touch ($1,000) and the Barista Pro ($850). And it’s the one that best mixes full-flavored, nuanced espresso with the ease of machine-guided, touchscreen operation. It’s versatile, it’s powerful, its PID controller means the brew temperature is quite stable, and it makes absolutely lovely cups—espresso that’s denser and more intensely aromatic than the coffee made by any other machine on this list, whether in bringing out the fruity berry notes in an anaerobic light roast or the dark chocolate of a roasty Italian.

In the finicky, often difficult world of classic home espresso machines, the Oracle Jet is a paragon of simplicity and machine-guided brewing: It’s a miracle that one can so easily pull such delicious and nuanced shots that remain so sensitive to the character of each bean. But that sensitivity still makes the Oracle Jet a little more finicky than other machines on this list. And while the automatic milk frothing is quite good, it’s not as failsafe as our favorites here. (I still like steaming milk manually on the Breville, versus using the auto-froth.)

Which is to say that as a latte machine, this Breville is all about the espresso. If you want espresso that will distill the beauteous character of fresh-roasted beans but still don't want to try overly hard—on a machine whose intuitive touchscreen tutorial will guide you to lovely flat whites and capps? This is your huckleberry.

For those who’d rather not fuss with beans at all but still want a lovely milk-frothed latte and cappuccino in the morning, there is this clever two-piece setup from Nespresso—with “espresso” on one machine via Vertuo coffee pods and an Aeroccino milk frother that’s whisper-quiet and will whip you up some milk foam in a minute. The espresso that comes from pods is not quite espresso, of course, but WIRED reviewer Louryn Strampe loved it best of all pod espresso machines, with excellent body and mouthfeel and especially ease. The Vertuo Pop+ will also make a drip-coffee-style mug.

But this frother bundle generally offers you a good bargain on an all-in-one system, and the Aeroccino is in the upper echelon of milk frothers WIRED has tested. (Note, however, you'll have to plug in each machine separately.) This said, if you want the ease of pod espresso but are fussy about your milk, you may want to grab a stand-alone Vertuo Pop+ ($129) and the excellent Dreo Baristamaker ($100). Do this when a good sale is running, and you might cobble this together at a similar price to the Aeroccino bundle.

The Aeroccino was easy to use—pour in your milk of choice and press the button. it will heat and froth your milk automatically—it takes about a minute, and it’s whisper-quiet. Every Nespresso capsule I’ve tried has featured a thick layer of crema, and having whipped, thick milk on top of it made my average cup of coffee a more elevated experience.

Sometimes making a whole latte or cappuccino using an automated machine can be a time suck. Not to mention, sometimes all you really want is frothy milk. That’s where milk frothers come in. These machines beat air into milk, or milk substitutes, to get that nice creamy froth. Former WIRED Reviewer Jaina Grey loved this handheld from Subminimal, a highly specialized immersion blender that makes properly textured, creamy, light, airy, wonderful milk. One screen makes fine-textured milk. One makes “ultra-fine.” Note that Subminimal has also added a milk frothing pitcher called the Nanofoamer Pro ($159) that costs a bit more, but is currently sitting prettily atop our guide to the Best Milk Frothers.

This streamlined machine from relative newcomer Terra Kaffe is a pleasant surprise, given the complexity of Terra Kaffe's first machine, the superautomatic TK-02 (see below), which bristled with features and doohickeys. The Demi is perhaps the dead-simplest fully automatic espresso machine I've yet encountered that still makes good coffee. If you don't want to customize your shot, there's just a dial and a button: espresso, lungo, Americano, drip, hot water, bye!

You can click into submenus and edit these to a nerd's content, both by volume and strength. You can adjust among five grinder settings as well—a low but relatively typical number of settings for automatic machines that already grind coarser than espresso machines with portafilters. You may need to futz with grind and dose strength to get good results with light roast, especially on espresso, but with a good medium roast, the Terra Kaffe offers a very smooth ride. Honestly, this is the machine I'd put in a front room for customers to use if I owned a small business. Super easy, no fuss, good for multiple types of people—and the reservoir is big enough at 1.4 liters that you won't be refilling the water all day.

But note that this is actually not a latte machine: It's only half of one. There's no milk frother. Luckily, the world is full of good milk frothing jugs these days, and we especially recommend the Subminimal Nanofoamer Pro ($159), WIRED's favorite milk frother.

Ninja has a habit of taking high-falutin', pro-level, or commercial equipment—whether soft-serve ice cream machines or slushie machines—and finding a way to make it easy, accessible, fun, and probably viral on TikTok. WIRED contributing reviewer Tyler Shane was skeptical about Ninja's first foray into the latte and cappuccino world with the Luxe Cafe Premier (7/10, WIRED Recommends), especially since the machine also promised cold brew and even traditional drip coffee. But she came away impressed.

This Ninja is not a superautomatic machine like our top automated pick, the Rivelia. It's what the industry likes to call “semiautomatic.” Semiautomatic espresso machines offer a built-in grinder and automatic milk frother but still use a non-pressurized portafilter that will pull a classic espresso shot with full nuance and aromatics. In our espresso maker guide, we recommend the ever-reliable and terrific Breville Barista Express ($700) as WIRED's favorite accessibly priced semiautomatic. But this Ninja is the machine I'd probably give to a beginner, a new college grad, or anyone whose first priority is ease and great automatically foamed milk

The drip coffee is meh, granted. But more than perhaps any semiautomatic machine in its price range, the Ninja Cafe Luxe Premier is geared to absolute ease and versatility—with an intuitive digital user interface that helps you along. Depending on your chosen drink, the Ninja Luxe will recommend the appropriate grind size on its display screen and help you dial it in. (This may take a couple of tries.) Milk frothing is easy, and the automatic milk frothing is shockingly good. Plus, you can froth cold foam, for silly cold-foam drinks. See what I mean? Ninja is fun. That said, we ended up preferring the Luxe Cafe Pro ($750), which costs a little more but adds a welcome auto-tamper and hot water spout.

This superautomatic espresso machine is one of the few coffee machines made by German auto and appliance behemoth Bosch. It is both highly sophisticated and a bit of an odd duck—capable of making an unholy variety of espresso drinks downloaded via firmware. The milk system is especially interesting, and for some, it may be the biggest selling point. On the base model, the milk system is basically a tube you attach to the side of the brew head. You can stick the other end of the tube in any container, and it'll steam whatever milk you've got directly into your cup before adding the espresso. This is great for families who use multiple milks. It's also great for not wasting milk.

The espresso is similar to superautomatics from De'Longhi, which is to say it's a smoother, more rounded, but less nuanced take on espresso that's great for milk drinks. But the “drip” is also interesting. The Bosch 800 “slow brew” coffee—while it does not have the clarity or brightness of drip coffee— is perhaps my favorite drip coffee from an espresso machine, round and roasty and lovely. It extracts only the smooth, chocolate end of the coffee spectrum. I haven't tested the pH, but it seems quite low in acidity. It's nice.

But here are the caveats: Coffee cup height clearance can be an issue on milk drinks, the pump is a bit louder than some, it's slow to boot up, and some parts feel a bit flimsy or plasticky for a machine in this price range. Also, if you do want an attached milk carafe, it's hundreds of dollars more, depending on current deals.

The delta between home espresso machines and the commercial workhorses used by busy third-wave shops is still thousands of dollars, but that hasn’t stopped both beloved brands and scrappy upstarts from infiltrating the space with more approachable units. Skip the junk and level up to the Casabrews 5700PRO (7/10, WIRED Review), which offers an unfussy take on the art of homemade espresso drinks.

Instead of bewildering noobs with a million settings and onboard tutorials, this 12 x 11 x 16-inch tank of a machine keeps it simple with easily accessible controls for things like temperature and dose volume for extraction, and run time for the onboard grinder. It's a single-boiler machine, not a dual boiler, which means you can’t froth your latte milk at the same time as pulling a shot, but the texture of the frothed milk is perfectly malleable and up to snuff for a basic leaf or rosetta pattern.

The guide rails that hold the portafilter in place are a bit too close to the output spout of the grinder, and temperature controls that deal in absolute rather than relative values would be welcome improvements. But until Casabrews implements our feedback, this is still a solid unit that’s a great pick for anyone who’s ready to never leave their house for a cappuccino ever again. —Pete Cottell

The superautomatic Terra Kaffe is a pricey hunk of machinery and has its bugs, but considering its ease and customizability, it's worth the price, wrote WIRED contributing reviewer Tyler Shane last year. She praised the device's convenience, its ease, the front-facing water filter, waste tray, and milk carafe, and its excellent app (available for iOs and Android) that offers easy controls and the ability to warm up your machine from your bed or the bathroom.

Drinks like latte macchiatos, drips, and iced coffee can all be adjusted to your tastes, and a milk frothing dial allows you to adjust the milk’s texture from foamy to silky. For those who love true, real, drip coffee, that's the biggest selling point for the Terra Kaffe over our top automated picks, the De'Longhi Rivelia and the Ninja Cafe Luxe Premier: The TK-02 offers it. The drip coffee is also good enough that Shane cleared her Chemex pour-over carafe from her counter.

De’Longhi’s Magnifica Start is a no-nonsense superautomatic with a conical burr grinder, four preset recipes at the push of a button, and the ability to brew a smooth and potent espresso, wrote WIRED contributing reviewer Tyler Shane. As with other high-end De'Longhi devices of the moment, the milk frother is truly impressive, offering seriously luxurious frothed milk. Milk-based recipes at the touch of a button are a latte macchiato and a cappuccino, while espresso and Americanos are the espresso-based options. There’s a slot for ground beans and a hopper for whole beans. Figuring out grind size takes a little trial and error, Shane noted, and it's not an overly quiet machine. But the Start is compact and efficient, and priced far lower than our favorite De'Longhi automatic, the Rivelia. This makes the Magnifica Start a solid investment.

The key here is automation. We wanted to test machines that make you a cup of coffee with a single touch, or as close to that as possible. So the products on this list are all of the automatic and semiautomatic variety. You fill ’em up and they do all the hard work—or most of it, anyway. Nothing here doesn't have a milk frother that does the work by itself.

Setup and cleanup were especially important, as was durability. The entire point of a device like this is to save time and energy and/or produce a drink of higher quality than can be made without it, so we didn’t recommend any products that didn’t produce tasty espresso and save time.

In May 2026, WIRED’s UK team gathered four fully automatic machines—the Terra Kaffe TK-02 (above), Philips’ Café Aromis 8000 Series, De'Longhi's Eletta Explore, and Jura E8—and made both lattes and espressos for local industry experts to judge. You can read the results and watch the resulting video here. The Reviews team is currently testing the winner of that challenge, Philips Café Aromis 8000, to see how it compares against the top picks in this guide.

Even if you're not making espresso, the first and best thing you can do to dramatically improve your morning coffee is to buy locally roasted beans. Plug your city or region and “locally roasted coffee beans” into Google and you will be glad you did. The reason that your locally roasted coffee will taste worlds better than anything you'd buy from a major coffee roaster (like Starbucks, Illy, or Gevalia) is simple: Good coffee starts to lose flavor the moment it's roasted. Get it fresh and you're giving yourself a much better chance at high-quality espresso.

Want some help finding the best roasters? For some of our favorite mail-order brands, with beans often roasted the same day or week they're placed in the mail, check out our roundup of the Best Coffee Subscription Services.

I hate to break it to you, but pre-ground coffee from a supermarket bag is pretty much always worse. Unless you see a roasting date on the bag, you probably have no idea when the roaster actually roasted it. If the roaster is a French or Italian brand, there's a good chance it was months ago. Coffee is best when it's fresh, ideally brewed a week or two after it's roasted. And grinding the beans dramatically increases the rate at which coffee degrades. This doesn't just affect how the coffee tastes. It affects how well the espresso maker will push water through the beans, leading to possible blowouts or bad extraction.

If you haven’t made espresso before and you don't have access to a coffee grinder, we recommend you buy locally roasted beans. Just ask your local coffee roaster for a fine (espresso) grind. We've tried a lot of pre-ground espresso blends from popular companies like Lavazza, Gevalia, and Café Bustelo. They were all very dark and very bitter, partially because they are all either imported or roasted in big batches and shipped all over the world. Pre-ground coffee will always be a little stale, and it's hard to get a good cup from coffee that's started to degrade—which happens fast after you grind it.

Get it ground fresh from a local roaster, and you'll have about a two-week window before you'll notice any difference. Many of the machines recommended here come with a grinder, so whole beans are already the best choice. But our roundup of The Best Coffee Grinders can also provide some guidance here, if you want to get into the grinding game, buy whole beans, and keep your coffee tasting its best.

Look, milk is milk. Anything that contains milk has the potential to get strange over time, and this includes the milk containers and milk frothers on automatic espresso machines. WIRED's previous espresso reviewer, Jaina Grey, was extremely sensitive to this issue—devoting her time to dishwashering, soaping, scrubbing, and otherwise testing the best methods for making sure that milk containers on automatic espresso machines remain sacrosanct environments.

Regular washing is, of course, the first and best recourse. But occasionally, you'll also want to sterilize your milk reservoir and milk frother.

First, hand-wash it with soap and water as usual, and make sure you get a sponge into those corners. Next up, there are a couple of options. The most effective will be a food-grade sanitizer like Star San, or One Step. Essentially, just make a dilution per the instructions on either product, pour that into a spray bottle, give the inside of the milk container a couple of sprays, and let it dry on a drying rack.

The second-best option, the one that uses things you probably have in your house right now, is a mix of distilled white vinegar and plain old tap water. If you have staining or really stubborn smells, you'll want to let it soak. Try adding about one shot glass (1.5 ounces) of distilled white vinegar and fill the container up the rest of the way with warm water. Let it soak for about 30 minutes, then rinse it out till there's no more vinegar smell, and you should be good to go.

#304. Retail turnarounds are taking hold just in time for the holiday season

Once-struggling retailers are entering the holiday quarter with improved performance and sales momentum as turnaround efforts begin to resonate with shoppers.

A handful of earnings reports on Tuesday pointed to a mix of factors behind the strong results, including a resilient consumer, stronger execution and demand for the right products at the right price.

Kohl's reported comparable sales growth of 1.2% for the period ended Oct. 31 and raised its full-year outlook as CEO Michael Bender said customers "have remained resilient" but are "migrating to value with their purchases."

He tied improvement to the company's work on product assortment, store experience and value.

Best Buy also on Tuesday posted its highest comparable sales growth in five years, at 6.1%, which prompted the electronics retailer to raise its full-year outlook.

"We have a tremendous amount of momentum," CEO Jason Bonfig told CNBC in an interview. "The fact that we saw pretty much broad-based growth across almost all of our categories is a lot of momentum that we're very excited about."

The company also credited execution, market share gains and a compelling product cycle alongside growing customer demand.

At Dick's Sporting Goods, quarterly comparable sales rose 2.6% at the core business and 0.5% at Foot Locker. CEO Lauren Hobart said "all income demographics grew" and the company "didn't see trade-down from best to better or better to good."

She similarly pointed to new products and market share gains within the category as contributing to the strong quarter. She also highlighted continued improvement at Foot Locker.

All three companies have been undergoing efforts to boost sales and get the right products on shelves to meet customer demand.

Target, likewise undergoing revitalization efforts, last week reported comparable sales growth of 5.6% in the third quarter, fueled by a 5% increase in comparable traffic. The retailer raised its full-year outlook.

CEO Michael Fiddelke at the time called the traffic gain "a healthy sign that guests are responding to our changes and choosing Target more often."

Even Gap CEO Richard Dickson told CNBC the company has moved from "rebuild mode" to "turnaround mode" at its Old Navy banner, a sign of progress, albeit not a broad-based portfolio recovery.

Michael Baker, a retail analyst at D.A. Davidson, told CNBC he sees both a resilient consumer and company-specific improvements as driving sector strength.

"Retail sales have been more resilient than most think," Baker said. His analysis showed retail sales, excluding autos and gas, rose 5.1% in the third quarter on a nonseasonally adjusted basis — the strongest quarter since the pandemic.

But he cautioned that growth appears to be coming more from transaction size than traffic, with inflation, promotions and higher units per transaction driving up spend.

Dollar Tree, which reported better-than-expected earnings on Tuesday morning, posted a 3.8% increase to traffic, accelerating from 0.4% growth in the prior quarter, suggesting more shoppers may be bargain hunting. Comparable sales at the retailer increased 4.6% during the period.

"Consumers are under pressure, and they are increasingly selective about where and how they spend," said Dollar Tree CEO Michael Creedon on the company's earnings call. "When under pressure, shoppers prioritize value and buy closer to need."

Comparable sales of everyday essentials rose 8.9% at Dollar Tree stores in the third quarter, while sales of nonessential items were essentially flat, the company said.

— CNBC's Laya Neelakandan contributed to this report.

#303. Blade Runner 2099 finally takes this franchise to the stars

Blade Runner 2099 walks lovingly in the footsteps of Ridley Scott and Denis Villeneuve's preceding Blade Runner films, echoing their memorable cyberpunk settings and noir detective stories. However, there's one area where the TV show completely outpaces both films.

Like Blade Runner and Blade Runner 2049, Blade Runner 2099 takes place primarily in Los Angeles, rarely leaving the city outskirts. Its world is one of bustling streets, crowded apartment buildings, and the massive pyramids that tower over the Los Angeles skyline. Yet episode 2 opens with a different landscape entirely: a fiery red terrain bursting with rocky crags and rushing lava flows.

This is Namaka Moon, a real-life satellite of the dwarf planet Haumea. It's also the first time an on-screen Blade Runner project has been to space. (Notably, comic Blade Runner 2019: Off World has already blasted off to space.)

Space travel is a fact of life in the world of Blade Runner, as well as in its source material, Philip K. Dick's novel Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep? As part of larger space colonization attempts, humans are moving to off-world settlements. Who is preparing these settlements for human occupation? Replicants (or androids in the novel), whose enhanced strength and durability make them the ideal slave labor force for braving inhospitable outer space environments.

While off-world colonies seem prime for sci-fi exploration, they have just been a background world-building detail in the Blade Runner franchise. Billboards frequently tease the promise of a new off-world home, while extraterrestrial landmarks like Orion take center stage in Roy Batty's (Rutger Hauer) iconic "tears in rain" monologue. Neither the Blade Runner films nor the animated series Blade Runner: Black Lotus have ever left Earth.

That all changes with Blade Runner 2099's Namaka Moon opening. The sequence focuses not on what life in an off-world colony looks like, but rather the labor that goes into establishing one in the first place.

In the episode, replicant Olwen (Michelle Yeoh) clambers across the moon's rocky surface, establishing a series of beacons that shoot beams of light into Namaka's cloudy atmosphere. Once she leaves the moon, the beacons detonate in a series of spectacular explosions, presumably the first step in Namaka's terraforming process. As she tells companion replicant Marek (Johnny Harris), Namaka will be ready for human habitation in 20 years' time thanks to her work. Fittingly, the episode is titled "Birther of Worlds."

The Namaka sequence does a spectacular job of ushering Blade Runner into its own Space Age. But it isn't just a trip to space for space's sake. The entire episode opening is rooted in the replicant experience: the loneliness of traversing a perilous moon alone. The awe of watching a world come to life thanks to your handiwork. The hollowness of realizing you will never live in that world, nor be recognized for that work. It's key to understanding Olwen's character, as well as understanding the role of replicants in general. You could almost imagine Roy performing a similar task back in his day.

Plus, since Blade Runner 2099 has yet to show what an actual off-world colony might look like, it still leaves the door open for future Blade Runner projects to flesh out that aspect of the world onscreen. Clearly, the world is far, far vaster than just Los Angeles. Maybe Namaka is just the beginning.

#302. Study finds slightly higher risk of autism diagnosis in areas with more lithium in drinking water, but experts say more research is needed

A new study found a moderately higher risk of autism spectrum disorder in children born to pregnant people exposed to tap water with higher levels of lithium, but experts caution that this association does not show a direct link between the two.

About 1 in 36 children in the US is diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) each year, according to data from the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

Scientists still don’t know the exact cause of autism, a developmental disorder. Genetics may be a factor, but some have been looking at potential environmental causes, too.

Autism diagnosis has become more common, but pandemic disrupted early detection, CDC says

Cases may be on the rise, but that is also unclear. One study published this year on cases in the New York-New Jersey area found that autism diagnosis rates tripled among certain age groups between 2000 and 2016. A 2021 report found similar increases in cases, but the CDC says the increased number of cases is most likely linked to more doctors screening for the condition.

Lithium is an alkali metal that can be found naturally in some food and ground water. It’s used in batteries, grease and air conditioners, as well as in the treatment of bipolar disorder and some blood disorders. Its levels in US drinking water are not regulated, according to the US Geological Survey.

A new study, published Monday in the journal JAMA Pediatrics, found a small association between lithium and autism diagnosis in Denmark, where the researchers say the level of lithium in drinking water is similar to that in American water systems.

The researchers checked a database of people with psychiatric disorders for children born between 2000 and 2013 to find information on 8,842 cases of ASD and 43,864 participants who did not have ASD. They then measured the concentration of lithium in 151 public waterworks that served more than half of the Danish population and mapped out where pregnant people lived in relation.

For many neurodiverse people, 'The Sims' has been a lifelong comfort

As lithium levels in water increased, there was a modest increased risk of an ASD diagnosis. Specifically, compared with people at the lowest exposure level, those who had the second and third highest exposure during pregnancy had a 24% to 26% higher risk of ASD diagnosed in children. The group with the highest exposure had a 46% higher risk than those at the lowest level of exposure.

The researchers could not tell how much water the pregnant people drank, but they picked Denmark in part because residents there consume some of the lowest amounts of bottled water in Europe.

Experts say it’s important to note that the research can’t show that lithium exposure leads directly to an autism diagnosis.

Further study is required, said study co-author Dr. Beate Ritz, a professor of neurology in the David Geffen School of Medicine at UCLA, and a professor of epidemiology and environmental health at the UCLA Fielding School of Public Health.

“Any drinking water contaminants that may affect the developing human brain deserve intense scrutiny,” Ritz said in a news release. She added that the research would need to be replicated in other countries to look for a similar connection.

The implications of the findings are complex as far as public health policy is concerned, according to an editorial published alongside the study. Lithium levels in water, at concentrations that the study associated with a potential ASD risk, have also been linked with health benefits such as lower rates of hospitalization for psychiatric disorders and suicide.

“If all these of associations are valid, the wisdom of Solomon will be required to develop guidelines for lithium in drinking water that are maximally protective of the entire population,” wrote Dr. David C. Bellinger, a professor of neurology and psychology at Harvard Medical School. “Until the basic biology of ASD is better understood, it will be difficult to distinguish causal from spurious associations.”

'Heartbreaking' delays in autism diagnosis and treatment got even worse during pandemic

Dr. Max Wiznitzer, director of the Rainbow Autism Center at University Hospitals Rainbow Babies and Children’s Hospital in Cleveland, points to other research on the effects of lithium on pregnant people who take it for mental health disorders. Those studies – which look at people exposed to much higher levels than are found in drinking water – do not show a connection with autism spectrum disorder.

“It’s an interesting association, but causation is definitely not proven,” said Wiznitzer, who was not involved in the new research. “We have to see if there’s a viable and biologically plausible mechanism by which a small amount of lithium in the water supply can somehow do this, yet pharmacologic dosing of lithium in women with bipolar disorder has not been reported to be causing increased risk of ASD.”

Other studies have also suggested connections between ASD and environmental exposures to things like pesticides, air pollution and phthalates. But none of them points to any of these factors as a direct cause of the disorder.

Sign up here to get The Results Are In with Dr. Sanjay Gupta every Tuesday from the CNN Health team.

A link between environmental exposure and ASD is hard to prove, Wiznitzer said. With research showing that increased exposure to air pollution raises the risk of giving birth to a child with ASD, for example, he often wonders whether pollution is the determining factor or if it’s just the populations who live in more polluted areas.

“There’s a lot of speculation about about environmental factors, but how many of them are truly causally associated?” Wiznitzer said. “We are bombarded with a variety of environmental stressors in our everyday lives. We have to figure out how to basically safely navigate them, and this is probably not one that’s high on our list.”

#301. Secondhand shopping is going mainstream this holiday season as consumers seek value

As the high cost of living squeezes consumers' wallets this holiday season, more shoppers are turning to secondhand retail and thrifting.

The shift comes as consumers look for better value, buyers put more emphasis on personalization and younger generations change the way they shop. The U.S. secondhand apparel market grew 13% in 2025, nearly four times faster than the overall retail clothing market, according to GlobalData.

That segment is expected to reach nearly $80 billion by 2030, growing more than 7% annually on average, GlobalData found. Much of that expansion — 40% — was driven by Generation Z, followed closely by millennials.

"I think this has been their version of the thrill of the hunt that millennials loved during the recession days," Katherine Cullen, a global senior retail analyst at EY, told CNBC. "It's a way to really express an individual style, find something unique, something that really fits their own vibe and personality."

It goes beyond people shopping for themselves, Cullen said. With more emphasis on unique holiday gifts, shoppers are leaning more on secondhand retail than they have before, whether in clothing or in other retail categories.

They're looking for something that fits the personality of the person they're shopping for, she added.

For Vanessa Roberts, that meant finding two antique children's chairs that she says will perfectly round out her nieces' play space. Roberts, 37, said she's been thrifting for at least two decades, each time embracing the "thrill" of finding something unique or vintage.

Especially in fashion, at a time when the quality of mass-produced items has decreased, thrifted items offer more value beyond just the price tag, Roberts added.

"It's crazy that you can find better quality items at the thrift store right now from 20 years ago versus what you can find at stores right now," she said.

Roberts, who lives in Los Angeles, said she began shopping for holiday gifts in September. As she prepares her haul for December, roughly 70% of her gifting will come from secondhand stores, she estimated.

"It's been a fun little challenge, where it's like a little scavenger hunt when I go into the thrift store," she said. "I'm definitely thrifting for the holidays – I do it every year."

The trend coincides with an economy that has forced consumers to be more intentional about how they spend, as they face high inflation and elevated gas prices.

In October, the consumer price index rose a seasonally adjusted 0.4%, which was more than anticipated. Still, consumers are expected to continue spending through the holiday season, with sales projected to top $1 trillion for the first time — though some of that estimated increase is boosted by inflation.

"You have a consumer who, while they're willing to spend at the top level, they're willing to splurge selectively," Cullen said. "Consumers are looking for value, which I think is something that is making secondhand resale and re-commerce more attractive."

And while clothing is largely the entry point to buying resale, secondhand shopping is increasingly expanding into furniture, electronics and books, according to a report from consumer insights firm The Consumer Collective.

Its October report found that 34% of people surveyed said secondhand products offer better value than brand new ones.

Many secondhand items also have an inherent added value beyond the low price on the tag, according to eBay CEO Jamie Iannone. The uniqueness of those products, as well as the allure that vintage adds to them, means consumers may actually be seeking the benefits of secondhand in more ways than one.

"I can buy a product that's used, and it almost has cachet around it," Iannone told CNBC. "Consumers today, they're able to get these amazing values on products, and it's seen as very normal to be gifting pre-loved."

According to eBay's Recommerce Report in October, 70% of global consumers surveyed said they consider secondhand shopping important for managing their budgets. That same report also found that 89% of respondents plan to spend the same amount or more on secondhand products next year compared with this year.

Iannone said he thinks the interest in secondhand this holiday season is "much stronger" than last year.

"It's becoming just a more established part of consumers' shopping and gifting routines," he said.

At a time when algorithms are driving shopping trends, consumers are also looking for ways to distinguish themselves and their purchases.

That's stretching beyond buying for themselves to purchasing holiday gifts for others, too.

"Secondhand is where they're finding unique items to wear," Alon Rotem, chief strategy officer at ThredUp, told CNBC. The company's holiday survey found that respondents valued uniqueness nearly as much as the value of a thrifted piece.

"To me, that represents a pretty meaningful shift in consumer taste," he added.

It's partly why ThredUp, which is an online thrift marketplace, emphasizes that each of its products is "a snowflake," Rotem said — something unique.

That's the appeal of buying preowned, rather than purchasing off the rack that hundreds of other people are reaching for, too.

"Consumer tastes have changed, and they're much more into vintage," he added. "Uniqueness has a premium in their minds."

Larger retailers are taking note, EY's Cullen said. More retailers, such as Lululemon, Patagonia and Madewell, are dabbling in preowned.

Wall Street is also increasingly watching the growing secondhand trend. Though shares of some secondhand and resale companies such as eBay and Savers Value Village have climbed this year, shares of both ThredUp and The RealReal have tumbled year to date.

"There's a lot of conversation around authenticity or the best find," Cullen said. "I think that interest and momentum, along with some of the economic factors that we're all facing, the idea that people are looking to be frugal is going to just continue."

#300. 'I've lost her forever' — Why German voice actors are refusing to sign Netflix's AI contract

For decades, Germans have known Hollywood's biggest stars through the same familiar voices. Now an AI clause in Netflix contracts is splitting the industry over whether it protects performers or exposes them.

When does Cameron Diaz not sound like Cameron Diaz? When you're in a German cinema.

For more than 30 years, whenever the Oscar-winning actor has appeared on German screens, she has spoken with the voice of Katrin Fröhlich.

The same goes for all other famous actors. In Germany's €125-million ($138-million) voiceover industry, Hollywood's up-and-comers are "adopted" by a voice actor who provides their German voice — often for decades — ensuring continuity and a certain relationship to the stars for audiences.

But on Netflix, and perhaps elsewhere, many of those voices might be about to change.

Recently, Fröhlich and fellow voice actors Anne Helm (Margot Robbie) and Luise Helm (Scarlett Johansson) published a video on social media, letting their followers know they wouldn't provide their voices anymore.

The reason? They refuse to sign Netflix's contract, seen by DW, which contains a clause that lets the American entertainment giant use their voices for training its AI.

They're not the first voiceover artists to speak out on the topic. But they are the first ones to go viral.

"It was unexpected, completely," Fröhlich said. "For whatever reason, we managed to reach people, perhaps because … we are three well-known women in the voiceover industry."

"Over the years, we've managed to make good names for ourselves. It seems to have touched people that we made this statement together," she said.

The new AI clause has been in Netflix's contracts since January 2026. Voice actors sign one ahead of every production. It was negotiated by BFFS, Germany's union for film and television actors.

Fröhlich, like a significant number of voice actors, is not a member and feels as though the union went over their heads. However, BFFS says the deal gives them protection they wouldn't otherwise have.

Till Völger, an attorney and member of the union's board, says previous contracts and those with other streaming services are silent on AI or contain sweeping AI permissions.

If an AI-generated voice doesn't sound like a particular person, companies are free to use the data they have gathered as they wish. Training can take place in other jurisdictions and may not require the actor's consent at all, he pointed out.

"We have a massive, massive protection gap," Völger told DW.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Against that backdrop, BFFS argues the deal with Netflix is a step forward. It allows the company to train its own systems with recordings, but voice actors must give separate, explicit consent before their recordings are used to create actual AI-generated voices, even if the voice isn't recognizable as theirs.

"We've created a contractual right that the law doesn't provide," said Völger. "Is the situation perfect? No. Is it better than before? Yes."

He would like to see other streaming services agree to the same conditions that Netflix has. In his view, only legislation could create the necessary protections voice actors are seeking.

Netflix says human performance "is and remains important to us," in statement provided to DW.

"In recent years, we have commissioned thousands of hours of German dubbing, and we intend to continue supporting a similar volume of work and the use of human voices," the statement continued.

Matti Klemm, the voice of Jason Momoa and beloved children's cartoon elephant Benjamin Blümchen, sees things differently. Like Fröhlich, he is refusing to sign the new contract.

"In short, it says: as soon as I record something for Netflix, I'm automatically training their AI, for free," he told DW. "My job is to create a German original, a dubbed version with my performance, not to train the computer systems of some tech companies."

He is taking Netflix to court, backed by the Society for Civil Rights (GFF), to find out how his voice has been used for training in previous projects.

According to Davy Wang, who is coordinating the case for Klemm and GFF, the lawsuit will seek to stop Netflix using his recordings for training, disclose how previous data was used and establish whether Klemm is entitled to any damages.

The suit will be filed at the end of the year or in early 2027. Supporters donated more than €50,000 to the legal fund in the first week following its announcement.

For Klemm, what is at stake goes beyond training. "It's not about our voice, it's about our soul, our performance, the way we are," he said. "How far have we come when AI training matters more than my actual work?"

Netflix said it cannot comment on a case that has not yet been filed.

For a multimillion-euro industry, the outcome of the case could reach well beyond Netflix and other companies and creative branches are watching. But no matter what the outcome of the lawsuit or contract agreements, voice actors' fears for their future run deep.

Those who don't sign contracts can't work, and streaming companies can make up a significant part of their income.

"Many say: I've held out for 10 months, but I can't anymore. I have to sign this contract, I have to pay my rent, I have to feed my children," explained Fröhlich.

Beyond that, many fear the future of their industry and the connections they have formed with stars and audiences.

"For a many people I'm connected with Cameron Diaz and I evoke something within them," said Fröhlich.

But if Diaz is involved in more Netflix projects, "then I've basically lost her," she concluded. "I'll never be her voice again."

#299. Blade Runner 2099 sneaks in a book detail that never made it into the movies

As adaptations go, Blade Runner is a fairly loose take on Philip K. Dick's Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?

The 1982 film replaces the novel's androids (or "andys") with replicants. Characters from the novel were cut, including Iran, the wife of Rick Deckard (Harrison Ford), and John Isidore, who houses the androids Deckard hunts. (William Sanderson's J.F. Sebastian effectively replaces him in the film.) These are just some world-building details from Dick's work that Blade Runner couldn't fit into a feature-length film.

However, one of these missing elements just made its way into the Blade Runner 2099 TV series.

In Blade Runner 2099's sixth episode, replicants Julius (Tom Burke) and Clotilde (Amy Lennox) drive past a large billboard that advertises "the power of Mercer." The display is a reference to the fictional religion of Mercerism, built around the martyr Wilbur Mercer. Much of the rest of the episode takes place at the abandoned island Mercer Monastery where Cora (Hunter Schafer) grew up.

Mercerism was initially conceptualized in Dick's 1964 short story "The Little Black Box." Followers connect with Mercer by gripping the handles of an empathy box. This device allows the user to experience Mercer's climb to his death: a slow ascent up a hill during which he's stoned repeatedly.

Dick revisits Mercerism in Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?, in which Deckard uses an empathy box and sees visions of Mercer. However, radio host Buster Friendly exposes that the Mercer seen in the empathy boxes is simply a character played by an actor. Buster is omitted from Blade Runner and its sequel Blade Runner 2049. In Blade Runner 2099, however, he is played by Hugo Hamlet, and can be spotted in TV broadcasts.

Mercer plays a key role in Blade Runner 2099 episode 6, which is named "Kill the Killers" after Mercer's major tenet: "You shall kill only the killers."

When Cora and Olwen (Michelle Yeoh) investigate the monastery,  they encounter the lone Mercerite (David Dencik) living there. He's keeping up a religious telecast devoted to Mercer, and he claims the signal is strong enough to reach Los Angeles. But given that no one else has joined him, it appears his efforts are just shouting into the void.

The Mercerite has an empathy box, and he prompts Olwen to use it while he holds her at gunpoint. Within, she sees Mercer (Tomas Rydval) making his last climb. As unseen forces pelt him with rocks, the empathy box shocks Olwen's hands to mimic the painful experience.

Olwen eventually uses a loose handle from the box to stab her captor. Then, she and Cora escape the island without becoming Mercer converts. (Sorry, Wilbur.)

The episode functions both as a tribute to this piece of world-building and as a key subplot that was initially lost when Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep? leaped from page to screen.

Buster Friendly and Wilbur Mercer may not have gotten their time to shine in Blade Runner or Blade Runner 2049, but in a TV series like Blade Runner 2099, there is space to expand on the world and give them a moment in the spotlight, no matter how brief.
